executive_summary: EUR/CHF closed at 0.93258 on 2026-10-02. The pair is quoted in Swiss francs per euro, so a rising rate means a stronger euro. On the closing-price basis it sits at the 68th percentile of its 52-week range. Performance is -0.68% over one month, +1.08% over three, +0.84% over six and +0.52% over twelve. The headline numbers hide a sharp break. The pair spent September trying to reach its 200-week average. It failed for the 381st consecutive week, with a 0.94701 closing high on 11 September. It then lost 144 pips in two sessions, 1-2 October, as French debt stress turned into demand for the franc. Both standalone dossiers are bearish on their own currency: EUR scores -0.2651 tactically and CHF scores -0.3002, which is pair-positive. The bilateral pair therefore nets the two weakest legs in G10 against each other. The structural driver is the euro's 250bp policy carry over the franc. It is offset by the franc's role as the regional refuge for euro-area sovereign stress, by a 7-point current-account gap and by an unbackstopped French fiscal premium. The settled verdict is Neutral tactically at conviction 2 (score -0.0898) and Neutral strategically at conviction 1 (score -0.0190). Our caveat, stated as a disagreement and not as a re-score: evidence from after pass 1's inputs suggests the tactical lean is closer to Bearish than -0.0898 implies. That evidence is the OAT-Bund spread at 130bp on 1 October, against the 111bp pass 1 used, and the SNB's sight-deposit jump. But the SNB now appears to be leaning against franc strength around 0.92-0.93. The practical expression is a two-way range anchored on the 11-touch 0.9224-0.9309 support band. Carry should be held at reduced size, and franc-positive tail optionality is cheap relative to delivered volatility.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Both dossiers carry a REER-relative proxy, not a true PPP. The euro's BIS broad real effective rate is 103.34 and the franc's is 99.87, both for 2026-08. On that basis the euro is about 3.4-3.5% rich to the franc. The CHF dossier converts this into a proxy fair value near 0.9139. At today's spot of 0.93258 the euro is therefore about 187 pips, or 2.0%, above that proxy. This is a structural observation, not a timing signal. A 2% real gap generates no mean-reversion trigger on a one-to-six-month horizon. The level is not stretched in either direction. The pair is mid-range on its 52-week distribution (68th percentile) and only modestly rich on the real-rate proxy. The market is pricing the 250bp carry against a French risk premium, not fair value.

market_context.recent_regime: Through September EUR/CHF behaved as a carry trade. It ground higher on a 250bp differential and the ECB's 10 September hike, and put in its 52-week high of 0.94884 on 17 September. It never closed above the 200-week. On 1 October the regime flipped from carry to haven. The OAT-Bund spread reached 130.3bp as of Oct 1, 2026 on Banque de France and Bundesbank data, up from the 111.2bp pass 1 used. One market commentary put the shift plainly: the Swiss franc is grabbing the spotlight as a haven against European risk after concerns about France's debt situation hit the region's markets. The SNB's weekly data then hinted at a response: total sight deposits rose to 464.24bn from 456.8bn in the week to 2 October, while domestic deposits rose only to 433.12bn from 432bn. The pair now trades as a direct read on French spread risk, with the SNB as a probable buyer of euros on dips.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The annualised carry for a long EUR/CHF position is +250bp on the policy basis: ECB deposit rate 2.50% minus SNB 0.00%, both as of 2026-09-29. The executable roll on the CME 6S/6E calendar-spread cross is -295.4bp annualised (observed 2026-09-30) and embeds the cross-currency basis; it is not the policy differential. Carry-to-vol is 0.748 on the estimated 3-month implied vol (250bp / 3.342%), 0.52 on 60-day realised vol (4.84%) and 0.44 on 20-day realised (5.73%); on the funding-premium basis it is 0.61 and 0.52. The implied-vol ratio flatters the trade because the estimate runs low and predates the shock; if the 17.8% understatement holds, the policy-basis ratio is nearer 0.63. On delivered volatility the carry is respectable but no longer exceptional. Carry worked through September and was interrupted on 1-2 October by a classic funding-currency unwind in which the franc rallied against every major. One 53-pip ATR day is worth almost three months of policy carry, which is why this carry has to be sized on the tail, not on the average day.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The policy differential is 250bp in the euro's favour: the ECB deposit rate is 2.50% after the 10 September hike and the SNB policy rate is 0.00% after its fifth straight hold on 24 September. That makes the euro the carry leg and the franc the funding leg. The front end confirms the gap. The Swiss 2-year is 0.31% (2026-09-29) and the Schatz 3.20% (2026-09-30), a 2-year spread of about 289bp. The live 10-year spread is about 300bp (Bund 3.58%, Swiss 10-year 0.58%, both 2026-09-30). The payload's 271bp 10-year differential comes from monthly series dated 2026-08-01 and is not quoted as a live level. Over four weeks the trajectory can only hold or widen in the euro's favour. The only scheduled decision in the window is the ECB on 29 October, where a hike is priced at under 30%. The SNB does not decide until 10 December. The transmission is plain carry: EUR/CHF can absorb about 19 pips of adverse spot per month before the 250bp policy carry is erased. The tactical risk to this reading is narrow. A 29 October hold would disappoint the hawkish euro curve, but only modestly, because October is already mostly priced out.

tactical.what_is_priced: The euro curve prices about 70bp of further ECB tightening (Schatz 3.20% against a 2.50% deposit rate) but under 30% for October. The Swiss curve prices about a 50% chance of a December SNB hike and at least 0.75% by September 2027. Both curves price tightening of similar size, so the priced differential is roughly static. Over four weeks what remains is the carry, not a repricing.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the question is which curve under-delivers more. The euro curve carries about 70bp of further ECB tightening. The EUR dossier expects one more hike, most likely on 17 December, which would be an under-delivery of about 45bp. Lagarde calls the stance a 'measured response', and Schnabel says policy can tolerate a slower return to target. The Swiss curve carries at least 75bp of SNB tightening by September 2027. Against that, the SNB's conditional forecast of 0.7%/0.8%/0.8% for 2026-28 is explicitly built on a policy rate held at 0% across the whole horizon, and economist consensus mostly sees no move before 2028. If both central banks follow their own guidance, the SNB under-delivers by more, and the realised differential widens from 250bp rather than narrowing. That is euro-positive through both carry and expectations. The sequencing matters: the SNB decides on 10 December (quarterly assessment) a week before the ECB's 17 December projection round. Confidence is held at 55 because the SNB leg is genuinely contested. Lombard Odier reads the September assessment as opening the door to a December hike. September Swiss CPI rose to 1.0% with core at 0.5%, and the SNB's own path needs inflation to average 1.2% in Q4, so the risks to the SNB are skewed toward tightening if Q4 runs hot.

factors.horizon_split: The stance and confidence are the same on both horizons, but the mechanism differs. Tactically the edge is carry with no Swiss event to interrupt it. Strategically it is an asymmetry in delivery against pricing, which settles at the 10 and 17 December decisions. Confidence is not raised strategically because the SNB December outcome is close to a coin flip on market pricing.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: On inflation the euro area runs much hotter: August HICP was 3.2% (core 2.4%) and the September flash due 2 October is tracked at 3.8%. Swiss September CPI was 1.0% (core 0.5%). The headline gap is about 2.2 points and the core gap about 1.9 points. That keeps the ECB under more pressure than the SNB, which is euro-supportive through policy. However, the energy share of the basket is about 7% in the euro area against about 3.5% in Switzerland. So the same inflation gap is also the euro area paying a larger real-income tax on the energy shock. On growth the differential favours the franc: Swiss Q2 GDP grew 1.885% q/q and 2.63% y/y, against 0.6% and 1.2% in the euro area. Survey data run hot on both sides: KOF is at 109.1, a five-year high, and the euro-area composite PMI at 53.1, a 41-month high. Both have forward-looking weak spots: Swiss ZEW expectations fell to 2.6 from 12.1, and the euro-area ZEW missed at 25.8. Over four weeks these channels offset each other. A hot euro-area flash keeps the ECB's December decision live, but the market already expects that, while Swiss CPI printed in line with consensus.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the inflation gap persists but its composition matters. Euro-area inflation is mostly imported energy: core is 2.4% and falling, and negotiated wages decelerated to 3.0%. That is a real-income squeeze on a net energy importer, not a demand boom. Swiss inflation is low because energy weighs little in the basket. The SNB itself expects inflation to rise somewhat in Q4 and then decline through 2027 as energy inflation fades. On growth, the SNB sees 1.5-2% for 2026 against the ECB's 0.9%, and that gap favours the franc structurally. SECO's warning that half of Q2 Swiss growth came from volatile pharmaceuticals tempers it. The inflation channel argues for a wider policy gap (euro-positive). The growth and real-income channels argue the other way (franc-positive). Neither dominates, so the honest strategic reading is Neutral.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Adjusted from defaults of 0.10 / 0.05. The franc is the classic regional safe haven, and EUR/CHF is the pair through which euro-area stress turns into franc demand. Risk appetite therefore matters more here than for a generic cross: +0.03 tactically, +0.02 strategically.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: EUR/CHF is a moderate risk-sensitivity pair whose quote currency is a safe haven, so risk-off pushes it lower. The current regime is mixed, but it is turning in the franc's favour more than against it. The VIX at 16.07 is low and rising from 14.43, which on its own denies the franc a haven bid. Credit is moving the other way: US high-yield spreads widened 42bp in a month to 3.02%, and the US 30-year is at its highest since 2002. For this pair the more important stress gauge is European. The euro-area-specific haven channel, which the CHF currency brief puts at a -0.2 to -0.3 correlation between EUR/CHF and eurozone sovereign spreads, is active, with the OAT-Bund spread at its widest since 2012. That spread level is counted under Factor 8, and the dated vote under Factor 7. Here only the transmission is counted: euro-area stress goes into francs, not dollars. Gold fell 6% in a month, which weakens the shared-haven link. That is the reason confidence is only 56.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months EUR/CHF is unusually exposed to how the Iran war ends, and both outcomes hit the pair twice. A settlement that reopens Hormuz would lift the euro area's terms of trade and real incomes and also remove the franc's haven bid, which is strongly positive for the pair. A renewed closure would raise the euro area's energy bill and add a franc haven bid at the same time, which is strongly negative. The base dossiers put a settlement at about 20% and a renewed closure at about 15%. Talks continue, the US rejected Tehran's seven-day roadmap, and the remaining dispute is reported to be about sequencing. Credit widening against tight investment-grade spreads gives no settled regime. The distribution is wide and close to symmetric in expectation, so the stance is Neutral with low confidence.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the CHF short is the currency's structural resting state as a funder. Leveraged funds were net short in every cached tranche from April. The euro side has the larger overhang: a real-money long of 216,483 contracts that has started to shrink. Unwinding toward flat would be a far larger flow than the CHF short. Against that sits the second-largest-reserve-currency bid for the euro. There is no evidence of SNB intervention in either direction: sight deposits rose only CHF 2.84bn to CHF 456.8bn in the week to 25 September. The two books offset each other at this horizon.

Pass-2 note (context, not re-scored): The tactical unwind trigger fired on 1 October in the form of a French spread shock. Weekly SNB data for the week to 2 October show total sight deposits up about CHF 7.4bn with domestic deposits nearly flat. That is the pattern usually read as intervention. It is the first sign that the SNB is on the other side of the franc squeeze, consistent with the verdict's strategic note that the carry short gets rebuilt.

tactical.combined_positioning_signal: Speculators are short both legs, so the net pair signal is muted, but the stretch is lopsided. The CHF leveraged short is at its sample extreme of 12.3% of open interest, against an EUR leveraged short of only 3.2%. Implied pair positioning is therefore modestly long EUR/CHF through the short-franc carry, and the long side is the crowded one.
tactical.unwind_trigger: A French government collapse around the budget votes (first part on 20 October, final vote on 17 November), a failed Hormuz negotiation, or a VIX close above 24. Each of these turns on the eurozone-stress channel into francs and forces CHF shorts to cover into thinned open interest.
tactical.historical_analogue: The CHF currency brief's reference case is the January 2015 floor removal, when EUR/CHF moved about 30% intraday. Nothing like that is in prospect, but it shows that franc covering flows meet thin liquidity.
tactical.contrarian_case: The crowd is short the franc to fund a 250bp euro carry. Open interest has just fallen 22% while the leveraged net short extended to a sample extreme, and euro real money cut its long by 14% in one week. That leaves the long-EUR/CHF carry exposed to a squeeze lower on any euro-area-specific shock.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Neutral. A CHF short is the franc's normal state as a funding currency, and the euro real-money long is large but shrinking in an orderly way. Neither is extreme relative to its own structural norm.
strategic.unwind_trigger: A sustained real-money euro exit, such as asset managers falling below 150,000 contracts net long, or an SNB reserve-selling programme visible as a sight-deposit fall of more than CHF 10bn over four weeks.
strategic.historical_analogue: Repeated CHF squeezes during risk-off episodes were followed by the short being rebuilt as long as the carry differential persisted. That makes a squeeze a tactical event, not a regime change.
strategic.contrarian_case: The strategic contrarian risk runs both ways. A euro real-money capitulation would push the pair down. But if the franc is squeezed and Swiss imported inflation falls back, the SNB's tolerance for a weaker franc returns and the carry short is rebuilt. Without a regime break neither side has an edge.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The external balance favours the franc by a wide margin. Switzerland's current account is 9.2% of GDP (Q2 2026) against 1.92% for the euro area (Q1 2026), a gap of about 7.3 points of GDP. The net international investment position is CHF 986bn. Bilateral goods trade runs the other way: IMF DOTS shows euro-area exports to Switzerland of $195.8bn against imports of $139.5bn in 2024, a euro net goods surplus of $56.3bn. strategic.bilateral_analysis: At the strategic weight of 0.16 this is the heaviest structural factor against the pair. The euro area enters winter as a net gas importer with EU storage at about 70%, roughly 12 points below a year earlier. The ECB notes that wholesale gas prices pass through to retail inflation within one to three months. Every cold month therefore turns into an import bill and a terms-of-trade loss for the euro. Switzerland has no direct commodity export exposure, but it imports little energy relative to the size of its economy and earns primary income on CHF 5,564bn of foreign assets. Its surplus has proved robust to the same oil shock. The bilateral $56.3bn euro goods surplus with Switzerland is a stable structural flow, not a changing one, so it does not offset the energy deterioration at the margin. The net cumulative balance-of-payments flow over the winter favours the franc. Confidence is 60 rather than higher because a Hormuz settlement could remove the energy leg quickly, and because the Brent level itself is disputed between the two dossiers (see assumptions).

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: The euro area is a net energy importer. Oil up is negative for EUR. Natural gas (TTF) up is negative for EUR and is the euro's most important commodity sensitivity. Energy is about 7% of HICP, and the EU spent EUR 41.3bn on energy imports in July.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Switzerland has no direct commodity export exposure. It imports energy, but energy is only about 3.5% of the CPI basket. Its commodity link is gold, through shared safe-haven demand and a large precious-metals trading share of exports (39.9% of 2025 goods exports). Gold up is positive for CHF.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step 1, oil +10%: EUR is negative (net importer, larger energy weight), CHF is only mildly negative (half the basket weight, small energy import bill relative to GDP). Net, the pair falls. Step 2, TTF +10%: EUR is negative (gas-heavy heating and industry, storage at about 70%), CHF is only marginally exposed. Net, the pair falls more clearly. Step 3, gold +10%: CHF positive through the haven channel, EUR unaffected. Net, the pair falls. Step 4, a generalised energy shock also tends to raise risk aversion, which adds a franc bid. All three channels net in the same direction: higher energy and gold prices push EUR/CHF lower, and lower energy prices push it higher.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: The pair falls. The euro area's terms-of-trade loss and real-income squeeze are larger than Switzerland's, and any accompanying risk-off adds a franc haven bid.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: The pair rises. The euro area's terms of trade recover and the franc's haven premium fades. Lower energy also undercuts the market's SNB hike pricing more than its ECB pricing, adding a rates channel in the same direction.

The SNB's conditional forecast is built on a 0% rate across the horizon, and Schlegel stresses that the SNB gives no forward guidance, while the curve carries at least 75bp by September 2027. In September the SNB went back from its June 'increased' intervention language to the standard wording. That removes some of the official backstop against franc strength, which matters in a euro-stress tail for this pair. Lombard Odier reads the same September assessment as opening the door to a December hike, so the SNB's message is not clean. Inside four weeks only the ECB communicates (29 October). A hold with an upgraded risk assessment would disappoint the euro curve only modestly, because October is already mostly priced out. Neither credibility gap resolves inside the window.

Switzerland carries no comparable domestic event: no federal election falls in the window, and the EU Bilaterals III package is not expected in force before end-2028. The Iran thread is also currently negative: the US rejected Tehran's seven-day ceasefire roadmap and talks remain in limbo. tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the pair is a contest between one deep factor and several shallow ones. Policy & Rates at 0.24 is the only Bullish line. The ECB deposit rate of 2.50% against the SNB's 0.00% pays the euro 250bp of carry (about 295bp on the futures roll), and no SNB decision falls before 10 December, so nothing scheduled can narrow the differential inside four weeks. Against it stand five Bearish factors that share one root: euro-area-specific stress, for which the franc rather than the dollar is the refuge. Those are risk appetite (credit widening 42bp, carried at 0.13), positioning (a CHF leveraged short at its 12.3%-of-open-interest sample extreme, and euro real money cutting 14% in a week), the euro's energy-driven external deterioration, the French budget votes on 20 October and 17 November, and the OAT-Bund spread at its widest since 2012. The base and quote dossiers are both Bearish on their own currencies, at -0.2651 and -0.3002, so the standalone views largely cancel in this pair. That is the first reason the bilateral read is Neutral, not directional. What the bilateral lens adds is that euro-area stress routes specifically into francs, which tilts the residual slightly lower. The ECB on 29 October is the only scheduled decision in the window. With a hike priced under 30%, a hold disappoints the euro curve only marginally, and a hike would be a genuine upside surprise. What is priced is a stable differential and French muddle-through. Our edge is limited to noting that the dated event risk is lopsided against the pair while the carry continues to accrue. The path of least resistance is sideways, with downside gap risk around the French votes. Conviction is 2 because the score sits within a percentage point of the Bearish threshold and rests on several factors at 52-60 confidence, none of them decisive. It would rise if OAT-Bund widened through the October vote or if a CHF short squeeze began, and fall back toward Neutral if the French first-part vote passes cleanly. Pass-2 note on the settled verdict (publishable disagreement; the verdict stands as issued): The verdict names two triggers that would raise conviction: OAT-Bund widening through the October vote, and a CHF short squeeze. Both appeared within two sessions of the valuation date. Neither rests on this pair's own chart. OAT-Bund moved from the 111.2bp scored in Factor 8 to 130.3bp on official 1 October data, with reports of 140-152bp on 2 October. The broad CHF rally against every major on 1 October reads as a funding-currency unwind. Our judgement is that a fresh scoring on this evidence would cross the -0.10 threshold into Bearish. Against that, there is a new counterweight the verdict could not see: the SNB's apparent intervention in the week to 2 October. It argues the move lower meets official resistance in the 0.90-0.92 area. We therefore read the published Neutral as 'Bearish lean, officially floored'. The levels, stops and scenarios below are skewed accordingly, while the stance itself is left untouched.

Short-franc views are better expressed against AUD, NOK or GBP, where the carry is wider and the funding leg is not offset by a weak base. Short-euro views are better expressed against CAD or NOK, where the energy shock benefits the quote. EUR/CHF ranks near the bottom of both the EUR-cross and CHF-cross opportunity sets for a directional trade. Its distinctive value is as the cleanest exposure to euro-area sovereign stress.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net of -0.0190 is firmly Neutral. Three non-zero lines nearly cancel: the euro's policy-delivery and carry advantage (+0.1320) against the external-balance gap (-0.0960) and the fiscal differential (-0.0550). The other seven factors are Neutral. Weights sum to 1.00 and contributions re-sum to -0.0190. This is a genuine balance of opposing structural forces, not an absence of information. Mapping to conviction: a score at the centre of the Neutral band maps to conviction 1.
strategic.rationale: Over one to six months the pair weighs two structural arguments of similar size. For the euro, the 250bp policy carry persists. Both curves price about 70-75bp of tightening, but if each central bank follows its own guidance, the SNB under-delivers by more: its conditional forecast is built on a 0% rate through 2028, while the ECB is expected to deliver at least one more hike against about 2.8 priced. That leaves the realised differential wider, not narrower. For the franc, Switzerland's 9.2%-of-GDP current account against the euro area's 1.92%, a winter energy bill falling on a euro area with gas storage about 12 points below last year, and France's unbackstopped fiscal deterioration against a AAA Swiss sovereign all push the cumulative flow against the pair. The dossiers' standalone strategic scores, EUR -0.2700 and CHF -0.2566, are almost identical, so the bilateral view confirms that the two weaknesses cancel. The bilateral factors widen the distribution without shifting its centre. An Iran settlement is unusually powerful for EUR/CHF because it lifts the euro's terms of trade and drains the franc's haven bid together, and a French collapse or Hormuz re-closure does the reverse. What is priced is roughly symmetric tightening and a slow energy de-escalation; our relative-delivery edge is real but offset by the external-balance edge in the other direction. The decisive dated catalysts are the SNB on 10 December (quarterly assessment), which comes first, and the ECB on 17 December with projections, bracketed by the French final vote on 17 November and the heating season. There is no path of least resistance in either direction. Conviction is 1: the score is close to zero and the largest single Bullish input, SNB under-delivery, is contested by Lombard Odier's hawkish reading and by a Swiss CPI path that needs a 1.2% Q4 average.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: On the dossiers' strategic scores EUR (-0.2700, 7th of 11) and CHF (-0.2566, 9th of 11) are within 0.014 of each other, so EUR/CHF is the least directional pairing of either currency. Strategic franc shorts are better held against NOK, SEK or JPY, which have Bullish dossier views. Euro shorts are better held against CAD or NOK, which benefit from the energy shock. EUR/CHF ranks last among the major EUR and CHF crosses as a directional strategic trade. Its use is as a carry holding with known euro-stress tail risk, not as a view on direction.

October and November belong to France: the pair should trade 0.9200-0.9400 between the 20 October and 17 November votes, with the 11-touch band as the floor the SNB appears willing to defend. December is the hinge. The SNB on 10 December comes first, then the ECB on 17 December, on the year-end funding turn. The declining 200-week reaches about 0.9423 by end-Q1 2027 and merges with the 5-touch 0.94217 shelf to form a single, lower ceiling. Upside beyond 0.945 therefore needs an energy settlement, not just carry. Expect two or three 100-200 pip swings around the dated events rather than a trend, with realised vol staying in a 4.5-6% band.

consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Pass 1: direction only; UBS implies about 0.8-1.9% of EUR/CHF upside from the payload spot to end-2026, while our view carries no expected directional move. Pass 2: our 0.9300 base is 100-200 pips below UBS at the six-month point and 200-300 pips above the haven camp's 0.90-0.91.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: UBS's case rests on better euro-area growth and higher real yields outside Switzerland, which is the carry argument we also score as Bullish under Factor 1. We differ in weighting three bilateral channels that a growth-and-carry case underweights. First, the euro area's winter energy exposure, with storage about 12 points below last year, falls entirely on the base currency. Second, French fiscal stress has no TPI ceiling and routes specifically into francs. Third, Switzerland's 7-point current-account advantage is priced at zero in the forwards. Together these offset the carry. Pass-2 additions: the street has moved toward our side since 1 October. One forecaster reports that the 0.9330-0.9500 corridor has been broken on the downside and it is lowering it to 0.9150-0.9400, and a broker note recommends short positions on EUR/CHF on upswings with targets of 0.9200 and 0.9000. Against the haven camp we are higher because the SNB's demonstrated willingness to act near 0.90-0.91 caps that path; in March the SNB issued an unsolicited statement saying it is increasingly prepared to intervene after the Iran crisis pushed EUR/CHF to an 11-year low near 0.9030, and the latest weekly data point the same way.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the energy and French risks materialise, a pair priced for modest euro gains disappoints. If they do not, carry still accrues to a long position at 250bp, so a Neutral view gives up little.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: A Hormuz settlement plus a clean French budget would vindicate the bullish consensus quickly, because both drivers hit the two legs of the pair in the same direction. That is the scenario in which our Neutral view most clearly understates the euro.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Both horizons are Neutral, but at different distances from the threshold. The tactical score of -0.0898 leans lower because dated euro-area stress events, the French votes on 20 October and 17 November, fall inside the window while the euro's offsetting positives do not. The strategic score of -0.0190 is close to zero because the two-sided Iran outcome and the December delivery question are both resolved over the longer horizon. Carry is the constant on both horizons.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 10 December SNB quarterly assessment, followed by the 17 December ECB projection round. A hold with no SNB tightening signal against an ECB hike would turn Factor 1 decisively Bullish and could move the strategic score above +0.10.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: There is no directional edge to trade. Carry exposure can be held, but sizing should reflect euro-stress tail risk around the October and November French votes, not the low estimated vol. The December decision pair is where a directional view could form. Pass-2 trading note: in practice the horizons diverge in risk, not in stance. The tactical window contains the event that can break the 11-touch band, the 20 October vote. The strategic window contains the events that can lift the pair back toward the 200-week, the December decision pair. Defined-risk downside optionality through late October, combined with a small strategic carry holding re-assessed after 17 December, matches that sequencing.

catalysts.event: SNB weekly sight deposits (weekly; next prints 2026-10-12, 2026-10-19)
catalysts.rationale: A rise of this size in total sight deposits, with the domestic component essentially flat, is the signature the market reads as SNB foreign exchange intervention. Sustained weekly rises would put an official bid under EUR/CHF near the 11-touch band. Weekly data are noisy, however: at higher frequencies changes in sight deposits are very noisy, and monthly movements are heavily influenced by short-term liquidity management operations, government cash flows and other factors unrelated to foreign exchange intervention. (Bullish if increases persist.)
This is the monthly cross-check on the weekly intervention proxy. August reserves were CHF 770.1bn. A rise beyond valuation effects would corroborate the sight-deposit signal of an official floor.

catalysts.rationale: This is the nearest dated binary and the only realistic route through the 11-touch band inside the tactical window. One commentary notes that if the budget survives parliament, that grants at least a temporary reprieve. A failure would extend OAT-Bund from the 130-150bp area, and the franc is the regional refuge.

There is no direct bilateral bias. The channel is risk and funding: a hawkish surprise that widens credit would weigh on CHF-funded carry. Weak US payrolls have since hit Fed hike bets, which is marginally supportive of carry stability.

This is the only scheduled policy decision for either leg inside the tactical window. A hike to 2.75%, priced at under 30%, would widen the gap to 275bp and lift the pair. A hold is the base case. French stress makes a hike less likely, because every hike tightens France.

catalysts.event: Swiss October CPI (week 1 of November; exact date not specified)
catalysts.rationale: This is the second of the two prints that decide December SNB pricing. A reading at 1.2% or above validates the hawkish read and threatens the carry case. A reading at 0.8% or below supports the SNB-on-hold path.

catalysts.event: French National Assembly final vote on the 2027 budget
catalysts.rationale: This is the widest-distribution euro-area binary of the horizon. The ECB backstop is not clean: the ECB does have a bond-buying backstop known as the TPI, but France would not meet its fiscal criteria, so any rescue would be a political decision rather than a market fix.

catalysts.rationale: It falls at the start of the December cluster and on the year-end funding turn. A hawkish outcome combined with balance-sheet constraints is the configuration that squeezes funding currencies such as the franc higher.

This is the decisive event for Factor 1's strategic Bullish stance, and it comes a week before the ECB. A hold that again builds the forecast on a 0% rate would unwind priced Swiss tightening (Bullish on a dovish hold). A hike or a normalisation reference inverts the carry case (Bearish on a hike).

catalysts.rationale: This is the likeliest venue for the one further ECB hike, which would take the gap to 275bp (Bullish against an SNB hold). It also forces the ECB to mark its EUR 51/MWh gas assumption to market.

Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes over the full stored history. The 200-week projection (about 0.9423 by end-Q1 2027) extrapolates the payload slope of -0.000222 a week linearly over 26 weeks.

Zone distances are the payload's own, measured to zone midpoints. Edge distances are stated separately where they matter: the 11-touch band's top is 17 pips below spot, and spot sits 3 pips inside the 8-touch band.

Implied volatility is the store's triangle realised-correlation estimate (3.43% / 3.342% / 3.449%), observed 2026-09-30, before the 1-2 October move. It is treated as a floor: the method understated EUR/CHF vol by 17.8% against Eurex. No quoted EUR/CHF implied vol or 25-delta risk reversal was located. The negative variance-risk-premium reading compares delivered vol with an estimate and should be read as directional, not precise.
Forwards are derived linearly from the -295.4bp CME funding premium, which embeds the cross-currency basis. Policy-basis points (250bp) are shown alongside. No quoted forward points were located.
Carry-to-vol ratios are shown on the verdict's estimated-IV basis (0.748, verbatim) and on realised vol (0.44 on 20-day, 0.52 on 60-day).

Rates: the payload's 10-year yields (EUR 3.18%, CHF 0.47%) are monthly series as of 2026-08-01 and are not quoted as live levels. Live front-end and 10-year levels come from the dossiers via the verdict.

Post-valuation research: web searches were run on 2026-10-06 and include items published after 1 October (OAT-Bund at 130.3bp on 1 October with conflicting reports of about 140bp and about 152bp for 2 October; SNB sight deposits for the week to 2 October; the September euro-area flash at 3.8%; forecast-corridor changes and 1-2 October commentary). These items are used for narrative, levels, catalysts and the stated disagreement, never to re-score a factor. The OAT-Bund figures conflict across sources and are presented as a range.
Scenario and invalidator probabilities are subjective, calibrated to the framework's 50/25/25 convention. They probably understate the franc's fat left tail for long-EUR/CHF holders.

IMF DOTS bilateral trade (2024) is used as supplied in Factor 5. The EUR-reported and CHF-reported net balances differ ($56.3bn against about $12.7bn), consistent with gold and pharmaceutical routing. The Brent level is disputed between the two dossiers.
Bank consensus combines the pass-1 UBS view with a May 2026 multi-bank survey located in pass 2. Ad-supported model-extrapolation forecast sites were found but excluded.

Formatter notes: the report does not state the dossier dates, so base_dossier_date and quote_dossier_date are set to the 2026-10-01 valuation date. CFTC percentile for EUR and the implied-vol percentile are not given in the report and are left null; the CHF CFTC percentile is set to 0 because the report describes the leveraged net short as the sample extreme. Catalysts dated only by week (SNB weekly deposits, Swiss October CPI, Hormuz negotiations) are given approximate calendar dates.
